title_original: At Paris Photo, Nature Bursts Its Banks
excerpt_original: Yellow. Everything is yellow, or almost. An American robin perched among red berries, a flock of starlings on bare branches, a young woman listening intently, her hand against her cheek. Alice Pallot spent the autumn of 2025 in New York on a carte blanche for the Éditions Louis…

blocks.text: Yellow. Everything is yellow, or almost. An American robin perched among red berries, a flock of starlings on bare branches, a young woman listening intently, her hand against her cheek. Alice Pallot spent the autumn of 2025 in New York on a carte blanche for the Éditions Louis Vuitton City Book, with the Tendance Floue collective. These images are on view at Hangar Gallery. Her subject: the “Birdwatchers,” amateurs who watch for birds in a megalopolis lying on a major migratory corridor that stretches from Greenland to the Caribbean. There are hundreds of them, she estimated (no one could give her a figure). There were the Queer Birders, the neighborhood clubs, the Linnean Society, and a visually impaired woman who made out, for the first time, a red spot: a cardinal. As the artist put it, these watchers “create a different way of being in and inhabiting the city.”

blocks.text: Slow down, then. That is the quiet watchword of a handful of images spotted in the aisles of the 29th edition of Paris Photo, which is celebrating the bicentenary of photography beneath the glass roof. Two centuries after the first heliographs, nature is no longer an innocent backdrop here. It is made to run, it is etched, gilded, stitched. Vertigo? Rather a form of courtesy.

“There comes a moment when the beauty of a landscape ceases to soothe.” The line is Letizia Le Fur’s, and it could hang as a sign over the whole fair. Shown as a solo presentation by Galerie Julie Caredda, her series “Les Monstres” (The Monsters) is the revelation of this edition: you come back to it, circle it, and walk away with your retinas still burning. Plants gathered over many years are assembled into digital collages: turquoise agaves under an ink-black sky, aloes in orange flames, cacti packed together like a crowd, blazing maples. The colors are pushed, sometimes invented, and the scales no longer match. “Some plants take over others, strangle them, smother them,” the artist wrote. In Cambodia, she photographed, with flash, a parasitic plant with salmon-colored filaments that wraps itself around trees. Who is the parasite, and of whom? “A parasite can also be very beautiful,” she replied.

Then the ink overflows. Working with her printer at the Dupon lab, Letizia Le Fur developed a costly process to make it run straight out of the printer. “I absolutely wanted these monsters to run and spill over the frame,” she explained, in order to “bring back a materiality to the print, and a bit of painting.” The teenager who used to copy Surrealist paintings is never far away: “What I like is to blur the lines.” The title, she specified, “does not refer […] to a creature but to a process,” and it also points to the monsters our societies create, ideologies, fears, power struggles, until they grow out of control. Too beautiful to be honest? The critic Claire Luna settled the question: this beauty “does not plead innocence.” Letizia Le Fur, for her part, embraces seduction as a weapon, a “manifesto: joy, beauty, kindness,” in the face of “a world that is a little harsher, especially right now.” Asked where she wants to go, she gave a one-word answer: “Everywhere.”

blocks.text: Richard Pak has come across monsters of a very real kind. On view at Galerie Spot, the French photographer has devoted a cycle to islands, “Les îles du désir” (The Islands of Desire). The first chapter, “La Firme” (The Firm, 2016–2017), took him to Tristan da Cunha, a volcanic rock in the South Atlantic where some 260 inhabitants have upheld, since 1816, a contract of equality and sharing made with the British Crown. The volcano, capped by a cloud, floats on a slate-gray sea. Then came “L’île naufragée” (The Shipwrecked Island, 2022–2023): Nauru, a tiny Pacific republic gutted by phosphate mining, which went from being the richest country in the world to one of the poorest in less than twenty years. At Anibare, coral pinnacles jut out of turquoise water like broken teeth. On his return, the photographer treated his negatives with phosphoric acid: the image suffered what the island had suffered. Of Tristan, Richard Pak said: “It is important for me to show that a society shaped on the fundamental ideas of equality and sharing does exist in this day and age.”

Masako Kakizaki, for her part, keeps her eye close to the ground. Originally from the Tsugaru region of Aomori Prefecture, the Japanese photographer earns her living photographing food (a tough school of precision) and devotes the rest of her time to landscape, shot on film in medium format. “I photograph landscape like it’s skin,” she told The Japan Times in 2018.

blocks.text: To this bare humility, Mineko Orisaku prefers gold. Born in 1960 in Ishikawa Prefecture, Miss Japan 1981, then a pupil of the photographer Shoji Otake from 1982, she prints her landscapes on gold and platinum leaf, a traditional craft of Kanazawa, the capital of Ishikawa. A pink weeping cherry on a gilded ground; Mount Fuji at dusk, watching over the port of Shimizu. “The cherry tree is a woman. Looking at it, it is very bewitching; you sense something of the spirits in it,” said Mineko Orisaku, represented by Nagasawa Gallery.

Gold again, but cold, in the work of Antoine De Winter. A Belgian doctor and anthropologist for eight years before studying at the Agnès Varda school in Brussels, he brought back the series “All the places and the places between” from a residency in Cadaqués, Catalonia. Cyanotypes on glass heightened with 24-carat gold leaf, prints made with salt from the nearby sea: a path winding between rocks across three panels, a sky as a diptych, a sea cut into tiles like cracked stained glass, a meandering river seen from above. Prussian blue and precious metal: the Mediterranean postcard turns into a reliquary. Speaking of earlier work on the Rhône Glacier, Antoine De Winter had already summed up the spirit of his method: “It was more a way of taking care than of showing or demonstrating.”

Fire, for its part, gilds nothing. At Laurent Lafolie’s, Galerie Binome, the forest has burned: Sicily’s in the summer of 2023, northern Portugal’s in August 2025. The French photographer, born in 1963 and regarded as one of the best printers of his generation, photographed these remains in black and white with a 4×5 view camera, before handing the images over to a laser. Not a drop of chemistry: the beam engraves recycled cardboard for twenty-four hours, and its burn advances as slowly as the fire that consumes. Hence the series “.BLANK”: charcoal trunks, hazy skies with no horizon, a bas-relief surface that vibrates, as if the destroyed trees were already beginning to be reborn from their ashes. You walk around it, and the image shifts.

blocks.text: A change of tools with Julie Cockburn, to whom the Brussels gallery Hopstreet devoted a solo show. Trained as a sculptor, the British artist hunts down anonymous photographs and embroiders them by hand, spending five to ten days on each piece. The 2026 vintage? A Polaroid agave with every flower retraced in green and yellow thread; a hand-colored Japanese bridge studded with dots like confetti ( Blossom Bridge 1 ); sailboats whose rigging turns rainbow ( So Far So Good ); a sea dotted with junks, from which threads stretch out like fishing lines ( Siren ); one tree grafted onto another, laden with pompoms hanging like fruit ( Fruitful ). Old-fashioned? Not for a second. “My work is about telling the truth, but in a really circuitous way,” Julie Cockburn explained.

Eight perspectives, the same restraint: not taking nature for granted. The birdwatchers taught Alice Pallot this in New York. There is, she said, “the idea that you can’t possess anything […] it’s really just the possibility of seeing a bird slip out of sight.”
